newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia forbids protest against Burmese leader.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia forbids protest against Burmese leader.

text.p: The Cambodian government and opposition leader Sam Rainsy appeared on Wednesday to be on a collision course over a planned demonstration against a visit by Burma's military leader.

Municipal authorities, citing security concerns, said on Tuesday they would not allow Khmer Nation Party president Sam Rainsy to stage a protest march Wednesday morning shortly before the arrival of General Than Shwe.

Sam Rainsy said late Tuesday he would hold the peaceful protest through city streets regardless of municipal opposition, however, adding that he and supporters would chant and carry signs reading, "Burma's dictator not welcome" and "Aung San Suu Kyi is a model for Asia."
"We will not remain quiet, we will not turn a blind eye," Sam Rainsy said at a news conference. "This visit is an insult to the pro-democracy movement around the world."

The Rangoon government has recently banned Suu Kyi, a winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, from giving regular weekend speeches at her home and blocked a congress planned for her National League for Democracy (NLD) party.
It also arrested hundreds of party activists and later released them in stages.

Than Shwe is scheduled to meet King Sihanouk, co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen and other officials during his first visit to Cambodia since diplomatic ties were restored in 1994, officials said.
Sam Rainsy said municipal authorities had sent him a letter banning the march, but said no reason was given for their opposition.
Municipality chief of cabinet Marth Chhourn told Reuters that his office had been told by the Interior Ministry that the protest should be stopped for security reasons.

"We have got a letter from the ministry asking us to do anything to stop any protest of any political party in order to ensure the safety and security of the Burmese leader during his visit in Cambodia," said Marth Chhourn.
A spokesman for King Norodom Sihanouk said that the palace had no comment on the controversy over the visit, adding that "We do not interfere in the internal problems of Burma."

Sam Rainsy, who met Suu Kyi in Rangoon two months ago, said, "When the Khmer Rouge killed millions of people, those who made protest -- should they be considered as interfering in Cambodian internal affairs?"
The Maoist Khmer Rouge is believed to have killed at least one million people through starvation, disease and executions during its rule over Cambodia from 1975 to early 1979.
